speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a positive sign which demonstrates the entrepreneurial spirit of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The 2017 Annual Business Survey conducted by the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry found that business sentiment among Singapore SMEs has risen.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, SMEs continue to face a number of challenges.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Rising business cost is also cited as the biggest challenge by 68.4% of those polled, ranking ahead of competition in the Singapore market and manpower shortage.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Government continues to help SMEs through various means, for example, through the SME working capital, and we just heard today's debate on the Enterprise Singapore Board Bill to support enterprise development, yet another example of helping SMEs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: SMEs themselves would have to continually evolve ways to deliver more productivity gains, for example, by leveraging technology.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One area that we could look closer at and where small businesses are particularly disadvantaged, is in respect of contractual dealings with large suppliers who dominate the market.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I will be referring to these clauses in the body of my speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This imbalance in power has allowed tenancy agreements to contain onerous clauses for tenants.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: An example of such a clause may be found in the handout.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I dealt with such a case some years back.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I acted for my aunt who ran a beauty parlour at a shopping mall for an initial period of three years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The mall owner extended her lease for another three years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: My aunt decided to spend money to renovate her premises.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: About 10 months later, she was served with a Notice to yield premises on the basis that the owner decided to renovate the floor in which her beauty parlour was located.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: My aunt was in tears as she had ploughed most of her savings into renovating the premises.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Not only that, she was upset that her staff who have been loyal and been with her for years would have to be let go, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Thankfully for my aunt, the High Court, in a reported decision, ruled that the owners exercised the demolition clause in bad faith.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For the vast majority of tenants in my aunt’s shoes, they have to yield their premises without any compensation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Additionally, commercial lease contracts include provisions stating that the tenant is responsible for any additional property tax that is payable on the leased premises above the base property tax payable by the landlord.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: However, if the shoe was on the other foot and the landlord subsequently receives tax savings through tax rebates, reliefs or exemptions, there is no contractual provision requiring the landlord to pass these tax savings to the tenant.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is also common for commercial leases to contain what I term as "illusory options".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: There are leases that provide that options to renew are granted on the basis of rent to be decided by the landlord at the time of the renewal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Another variation is the provision in the leases that the revised rent is to be determined by the landlord, whose determination is final and conclusive.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is unfortunate that despite the Singapore Business Federation’s (SBF's) laudable attempt to address this situation by issuing the Fair Tenancy Framework that was put together by its Rental Practices Working Group chaired by Ms Cynthia Phua, a former Parliamentarian, in 2015, the usage of these onerous clauses still subsists.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Besides tenancy contracts, other examples of contracts which may contain unfair clauses include contracts for the provision of utilities or telecommunication services.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I have provided an illustration of such clauses in the same handout that I distributed earlier in the House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For such contracts, small businesses are often in no better position than individual consumers in that they have little bargaining power to negotiate contract on the supplier’s standard terms.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Presently, in Singapore, small businesses are given some protections when entering into standard form contracts under the Unfair Contract Terms Act (UCTA).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: However, UCTA protections focus mainly on certain types of clauses, such as exclusion of liability clauses and indemnity clauses, which must be reasonable in order to be enforceable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Even then, certain types of contracts are excluded from UCTA, such as contracts that involve property interests.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In a report for the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) written by the Centre for Competition Policy in the United Kingdom (UK) in 2014, the report recognised two key arguments in favour of providing greater protections for small businesses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The first is that small businesses, which may not be as sophisticated and have the same level of resources as large companies, need protection to make effective purchasing decisions relative to larger businesses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Second, as a matter of policy coherence, if small businesses behave more like individual consumers than they behave like large businesses, then it would be coherent to treat them the same under the law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In Hong Kong, small businesses may rely on the Control of Exemption Clauses Ordinance, which is the equivalent of our UCTA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: However, unlike Singapore, for consumers, which by definition excludes small businesses, there is also recourse to the Hong Kong Unconscionable Contracts Ordinance (UCO).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The UCO provides that with respect to a contract for the sale of goods or supply of services in which one party deals as a consumer, where the court finds any part of the contract to have been unconscionable in the circumstances when the contract was made, the court may refuse to enforce that part of the contract, or limit the application of the unconscionable part.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Hong Kong UCO vis-à-vis consumers is, therefore, wider in its application compared to Singapore's UCTA in that it applies to all contractual clauses and not merely exclusion or indemnity clauses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Hong Kong UCO was modelled after the Australian Trading Practices Act of 1974 which applied to both small businesses and consumers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The United States (US) and Germany have also legal provisions that render one-sided contracts with small businesses unenforceable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Article 138 of the German Civil Code, known as BGB, renders a legal transaction, where a person exploiting the counterparty's weakness grants to himself a pecuniary advantage which exceeds the value of performance to such an extent that under the circumstances, the pecuniary advantage is an obvious disproportion to the performance, void.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Section 2-302(1) of the Uniform Commercial Code of the US provides that if a court, as a matter of law, finds a sale contract or any clause of a sale contract to have been unconscionable at the time it was made, the court may refuse to enforce the contract, amongst other options.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This provision has been judicially interpreted to apply outside the arena of sale contracts to lease of chattels, insurance contracts and other areas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The current UK position is similar to Singapore’s in that only legislative protection afforded to small business is through the UK UCTA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The main tranches of consumer law, such as the Consumer Rights Act 2015, which offers the most significant protections, only cover individual consumers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: However, there is some sectoral protection of small business customers in the UK by the regulators.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For example, under the 2003 Communications Act, a distinction is drawn between "domestic and small business customers" and other customers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Consistent with this, the UK telecommunications regulator, Ofcom, provides such small businesses with the same protection as domestic customers throughout its general conditions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For example, both types of customers are covered by Ofcom rules relating to information to be provided at the point of sale, the ban on automatic rollover contracts and restrictions on misleading or aggressive selling.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Each supplier is required to develop and publish a Code of Practice for both individual and small business consumers that should, at a minimum, specify where such customers can avail themselves of necessary information.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Access to the Alternative Dispute Resolution scheme is also available for both domestic and small business customers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Australia has taken a robust approach to protecting small businesses through the Competition and Consumer Act 2010, and the Australian Consumer Law (ACL).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: ACL provides for a national unfair contract terms law covering standard form consumer and small business contracts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: ACL provides that a term is unfair when it causes a significant imbalance in the parties’ rights and obligations arising under the contract, and it is not reasonably necessary to protect the legitimate interests of the supplier, and it would cause financial or non-financial detriment to a party.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Terms that are determined by a court to be unfair are void.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Additionally, the Competition and Consumer Act and the ACL are administered by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, which may investigate alleged breaches of the Act and take enforcement or compliance action.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Apart from this, certain Australian states have also enacted additional laws for more sectoral-based regulations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For example, in Western Australia, most retail shop leases are regulated by the Commercial Tenancy (Retail Shops) Agreement Act 1985, which does not apply to leases to publicly-listed companies and which regulates commercial tenancy agreements.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For example, the Act prohibits the landlord from engaging in conduct that is unconscionable in connection with the lease.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The relevant factors to be taken into consideration to determine whether the landlord has contravened this section include the relative strengths of the bargaining positions of the landlord and tenant; whether the tenant was required to comply with conditions that were not reasonably necessary for the protection of the legitimate interests of the landlord; and whether any unfair tactics were used against the tenant.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is open for other regulators in Singapore, such as the Infocomm Media Development Authority or the Energy Market Authority, to adopt MAS’ practice and require the big players to provide fair dealing outcomes to their customers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It will make them more competitive and, hopefully, allow them to make an even bigger contribution to the vibrancy of Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah. 6.59 pm

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He has suggested a general protection approach through legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government is empathetic to challenges faced by SMEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The question is how should we approach this issue and what should be the underlying philosophy that underpins our policy and approach?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Even when we do intervene, we try as far as possible to have the right regulatory touch and avoid heavy-handed interventions that could lead to distortion or unintended consequences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This philosophy has ensured that our businesses, big and small, can respond quickly to market signals and adjust their business strategies accordingly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It has led to growth and good outcomes for all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In any economy, it is inevitable that there will be competing demands and different interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The question is how to strike the right balance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Take, for example, the sample clause on the option to renew, which the Member had handed out.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: From the landlord's perspective, what he wants is certainty.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He does not want to be put in a position where the tenant can automatically renew the lease without knowing what the rent is, as that would be unfair to the landlord.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The landlord would argue that his clause is fair because his revisions must be pegged to market rate, and the tenant has the choice not to renew and rent elsewhere.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, as Members can see, there are conflicting viewpoints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Of course, one can legislate to the effect that landlord must have a clause that option to renew will be on the basis of market rate, full-stop.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But that may not solve the problem as the tenant and the landlord may disagree on what the market rate is.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If they cannot agree, the tenancy will either not be renewed, in which case the tenant will still have to find new premises, which is the same position that the tenant would have been in if he had rejected the landlord's revision under the sample clause; or the tenant can continue with the lease, while both parties litigate the market rate, which will sour the relationship, and likely rule out a further lease beyond the option term, which may not be in the tenant's interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Of course, you can then have a clause that says that the option to renew will be on the basis of market rate to be determined by a third-party valuer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Then you will have the question of who should pay for the valuer's fees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I highlight this not to suggest whether the standard clause produced by Mr Murali Pillai is a good clause or a bad clause, but simply to point out that, in every situation, there will be different views on what is fair, and the answer is not always clearcut.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ideally, the contract should reflect a mutually agreed negotiated position, taking into account the parties' commercial considerations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Just as in the property market today, there exists a wide spectrum of landlords and tenants with varying bargaining powers, and in differing circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This makes it difficult to determine whether a particular clause is unfair or simply the result of a valid, albeit hard commercial bargain.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In making these judgement calls, the Court may run the risk of substantively altering the bargain struck between two commercial parties, causing uncertainty in the process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In fact, this has been one of the common criticisms of the application of “statutory unconscionability” in Australia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, should the landlords, which this legislation targets, respond by increasing the rental rate to address the added business cost, this might end up hurting SMEs even more in the long run.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, not having general protection legislation does not mean that there are no safeguards under our laws to protect against injustice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: General contractual principles, such as the doctrines of duress, undue influence and unconscionability, apply to all contracts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These doctrines have been applied by the Singapore Courts to prevent a contracting party from being unfairly exploited by the other, when entering into a contract.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In relation to the demolition clause highlighted by the Member, the High Court has held, in the case which the Member referred to, that such a onerous clause will be “usually interpreted very strictly” in favour of the tenant, as the Courts recognise that “premature termination of the lease generally imposes inconvenience, if not hardship, on the tenant”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The outcome of Mr Murali Pillai's aunt's case does, in fact, illustrate how the law, as it currently stands, allows the Court to protect against unscrupulous behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Fundamentally, the issue, as the Member pointed out, is that of bargaining power.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As such, the way forward for SMEs should be to strengthen their bargaining power through growing their businesses, bolstering their negotiating positions with the assistance of business and trade associations, such as SBF, ensuring that they have other options and alternatives while, at the same time, seeking out ways to raise productivity, reduce cost and maximise profits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government has many schemes and programmes which SMEs can leverage to achieve these outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These are alternative premises for SMEs to consider renting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: SMEs should also consider leveraging Government schemes to build business capabilities, innovate and improve productivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These support schemes all work together to assist SMEs in transforming their businesses by uplifting their productivity in developing new capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Therefore, SMEs which do not get the benefit of the savings from property tax in the specific clause mentioned by the Member can, nevertheless, access various schemes which will help their businesses as a whole.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: SMEs can also explore whether rental costs can be reduced through new business models.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: SME retailers, for example, might consider expanding through e-channels beyond the traditional “brick-and-mortar” retail shops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will reduce the need for physical space and, hence, rental costs and, at the same time, expand their businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: SMEs are encouraged to participate in the ITMs so that they can achieve their full potential for growth and profit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The best way forward is to promote entrepreneurship and help our SMEs grow bigger and stronger which would improve their relative bargaining positions, individually and collectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Resolved, "That Parliament do now adjourn." Adjourned accordingly at 	7.08 pm
